why: An in-order walk of the BST lists the keys in sorted order, and in a sorted list the values closest to target form a contiguous window around target's insertion point. Taking the kth closest is then a two-pointer expansion outward from that point, choosing the nearer side each step.
hints: What order do the keys come out in if you walk the BST in order? Where in that order are the closest values to target?
The closest values sit right around target's insertion position: grow a window from there, one value at a time, always taking whichever neighbour (left or right) is nearer.
In-order traversal into a sorted list (O(n)), bisect for the insertion point, then k steps of two pointers comparing target - vals[i] with vals[j] - target. O(n) time, O(n) space.
pitfalls: On a distance tie the smaller value wins, so the left pointer takes ties.
When one pointer runs off the end, keep taking from the other side.
target may equal a key (distance 0) or lie outside all keys.
